lead: Every network application is a pair of processes in two places: one asks for something, the other provides it. The asking side is the client, the providing side is the server. Choosing which side holds the data, who stays awake, and whether any single machine is in charge decides how the application scales, what it costs in rupees, and what breaks when one machine dies. This chapter sets out those choices; HTTP, DNS, mail and file transfer in the rest of the unit are just particular answers to them.
prereq: You need: Unit 1 for layering and protocol suites, and Unit 5 for ports and processes; chapter 6.2 turns these two roles into running code.

sections.h3: A client asks, a server answers

blocks.text: A network application is two programs in two processes on two hosts. One asks for something, the other provides it. That is the whole client-server idea; everything else is detail about how the asking is arranged.

The client starts the conversation. It knows the server's address, which is an IP address plus a port number (Unit 5), and it sends the first message. A client is usually started by a person, runs for a short while, and may sit behind an address that DHCP changes.
The server is the other role. It runs all the time, waits at a fixed address and a well-known port, and answers whoever knocks. The client must not need to know the server's schedule.

Traffic is lopsided. The request is small, like a name, a URL or a command; the reply is large, like a page, a file or a mailbox. So the server's upload link decides how many clients it can serve, not its download link.
HTTP, FTP, SMTP and DNS all follow this pattern. Only a few universities also teach SNMP, a client-server protocol for managing routers and switches. Each protocol has its own chapter later.

sections.h3: Stateless, stateful, and how many tiers

blocks.text: A stateless server keeps no memory of earlier requests. Every request carries everything needed to answer it. Restart the server and nothing is lost. Put ten copies behind a load balancer and send each request to any copy. HTTP works this way.

A stateful server remembers the session: who logged in, what is in the cart, which transfer is half done. The memory makes the conversation simpler but ties the client to one machine. Restart it and the session dies; share it across machines and you need a common store.

Tiers count the machines behind the client. In a two-tier design the server talks straight to a database. In a three-tier design a logic layer sits between them: the web server checks the request, the application server applies the business rules, the database stores rows. Three tiers cost more machines and more hops, but each layer can be scaled or replaced alone.

items: Stateless is cheap to replicate; stateful is cheap to design.
Two-tier is quick to build; three-tier survives growth.
The more layers, the more places a request can wait.

blocks.text: In peer-to-peer (P2P) there is no fixed server. Every peer is both client and server: it downloads pieces of a file from others and uploads pieces it already holds. The role depends on the moment, not on the machine.

Finding those pieces happens in one of two ways. A central directory (a tracker) keeps an index of which peer holds which piece. Peers ask the tracker, then exchange data directly. Lookup is fast, but the tracker is a single point of failure and an easy thing to block. A fully decentralised overlay has peers form their own network on top of the Internet and find each other by passing queries along, or by a distributed hash table that maps a file key to the peer responsible for it. Nothing central exists to fail, but lookups are slower and the overlay costs extra signalling.

Scalability is the real difference. In client-server the server's upload rate u<sub>s</sub> is fixed, so extra users only add queueing. In P2P every new peer brings its own upload rate u<sub>i</sub>, so supply grows with demand. The cost moves too: one big server means a capital bill in rupees and a bandwidth contract; P2P spends the upload capacity users already pay for.
T<sub>cs</sub> = max(N·F/u<sub>s</sub>, F/d)    and    T<sub>p2p</sub> = max(F/u<sub>s</sub>, F/d, N·F/(u<sub>s</sub> + Σu<sub>i</sub>))
blocks.where: N is the number of peers, F is the file size in Mbit, u<sub>s</sub> is the server upload rate, u<sub>i</sub> is each peer's upload rate and d is each peer's download rate, all in Mbps; T<sub>cs</sub> and T<sub>p2p</sub> are the distribution times in seconds.

spec.aria: Two timelines: client-server with three 5 s copies ending at 15 s, and peer-to-peer with one 6 s bar of 30 Mbit at 5 Mbps.

examples.question: A 10 Mbit file must reach 3 peers. The server's upload rate is u_s = 2 Mbps, each peer uploads at u_i = 1 Mbps, and each peer downloads at d = 2 Mbps. Find the distribution time for (a) client-server and (b) peer-to-peer.
steps: Write the data: F = 10 Mbit, N = 3 peers, u_s = 2 Mbps, u_i = 1 Mbps per peer, d = 2 Mbps per peer.
(a) The server must send N copies, so the server's upload sets a floor: N·F/u_s = 3 × 10 ÷ 2 = 15 s.
(a) Each peer must receive F bits at rate d, so the download sets another floor: F/d = 10 ÷ 2 = 5 s.
(a) Both floors must hold, so T_cs = max(15, 5) = 15 s. The server's upload is the binding term.
(b) The server must upload at least one full copy: F/u_s = 10 ÷ 2 = 5 s.
(b) Each peer's download still applies: F/d = 10 ÷ 2 = 5 s.
(b) Total upload capacity in the swarm = u_s + Σu_i = 2 + 3 × 1 = 5 Mbps. Total bits to move = N·F = 3 × 10 = 30 Mbit. So the swarm needs 30 ÷ 5 = 6 s.
examples.answer: The client-server distribution time is 15 s and the peer-to-peer time is 6 s, so P2P finishes 9 s earlier.
examples.check:
F = 10.0
N = 3
u_s = 2.0
u_i = 1.0
d = 2.0
t_cs = max(N * F / u_s, F / d)
t_p2p = max(F / u_s, F / d, N * F / (u_s + N * u_i))
print(t_cs)
print(t_p2p)

traps: Writing the client-server time as F/u_s alone. The server uploads N copies, so N·F/u_s is usually the binding term.
Taking the sum of the three P2P terms instead of the maximum. All three limits act at the same time, so the slowest one decides.
Thinking a server is a type of hardware. It is a role played by a process; one machine can run a web server, a mail server and a P2P client at once.
Calling HTTP stateful because logins seem to be remembered. HTTP itself is stateless; cookies and sessions put the memory back on top.
Confusing a tracker with a file server. The tracker holds only the index of who has which piece; the file data moves between peers.

quiz.q: In the client-server model, which side sends the first message, and which side must be always on?
quiz.a: The client sends the first message. The server must be always on and reachable at a fixed IP address and port.

quiz.q: Why is a stateless server easier to scale than a stateful one?
quiz.a: Each request carries all the information needed, so any copy of the server can answer it. Copies can be added behind a load balancer, restarted freely, and no shared session store is needed. A stateful server must keep the client's session on one machine or in a shared store, which adds coordination.

quiz.q: A 20 Mbit file is shared with 5 peers. u_s = 4 Mbps, u_i = 1 Mbps each, d = 2 Mbps each. Find the client-server and peer-to-peer distribution times.
A tracker-based P2P system and a fully decentralised overlay each fail in a different way. Compare them on one strength and one weakness each.
quiz.a: Tracker: lookups are fast and the index is easy to keep accurate, but the tracker is a single point of failure and a single target to block, so the whole swarm stops finding peers if it goes down. Fully decentralised: no single node can be removed to kill the system, but queries must be flooded or routed through a distributed hash table, so lookups are slower and the overlay spends bandwidth on signalling.

quiz.q: What separates a two-tier design from a three-tier design?
quiz.a: In two-tier the server talks directly to the database. In three-tier a logic or application layer sits between the web server and the database, so business rules live in one place and each layer can be scaled or replaced separately.

quiz.q: In the client-server model the server's upload link limits growth; in P2P it does not. Explain why, using the formula terms.
quiz.a: In client-server the whole file set must pass through u_s, so the term N·F/u_s grows with N while u_s stays fixed. In P2P the same term appears as N·F/(u_s + Σu_i); each new peer adds u_i to the denominator, so capacity rises with the number of peers and the time levels off instead of growing.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real deployments mix the two models: a content delivery network puts client-server caches near users, while the caches fetch from each other in a peer-like way. BitTorrent-style swarms carry game and operating-system updates because the publisher's bandwidth bill does not grow with the number of downloaders. Blockchains push the fully decentralised idea to record keeping, with no tracker at all. Edge computing moves the server closer to the client to cut round-trip time, a trend that shows up in 5G and IoT syllabi. Search for content delivery networks, distributed hash tables, and edge computing to go further.
